claim: Humans studies have implicated the anterior insular cortex (aIC) in subjective fear regulation.
source: Humans studies have implicated the anterior insular cortex (aIC) in subjective fear regulation and its abnormal activity in fear/anxiety disorders.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to human studies in the broader scientific literature.

claim: Abnormal aIC activity is implicated in fear/anxiety disorders in humans.
source: Humans studies have implicated the anterior insular cortex (aIC) in subjective fear regulation and its abnormal activity in fear/anxiety disorders.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to human studies in the broader scientific literature.

claim: A balanced number of aIC pyramidal neurons' activity either positively or negatively correlated with conditioned tone-induced freezing response.
source: Single-unit recordings revealed that a balanced number of aIC pyramidal neurons' activity either positively or negatively correlated with a conditioned tone-induced freezing (fear) response.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-unit recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Optogenetic manipulations of aIC pyramidal neuronal activity during conditioned tone presentation altered the expression of conditioned freezing.
source: Optogenetic manipulations of aIC pyramidal neuronal activity during conditioned tone presentation altered the expression of conditioned freezing.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Non-overlapping populations of aIC neurons project to the amygdala or the medial thalamus.
source: Neural tracing showed that non-overlapping populations of aIC neurons project to the amygdala or the medial thalamus, and the pathway bidirectionally modulated conditioned fear.
evidence: This claim is supported by neural tracing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The aIC-amygdala and aIC-medial thalamus pathways bidirectionally modulated conditioned fear.
source: Neural tracing showed that non-overlapping populations of aIC neurons project to the amygdala or the medial thalamus, and the pathway bidirectionally modulated conditioned fear.
evidence: This claim is supported by neural tracing and optogenetic manipulation data.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the aIC-amygdala pathway increased conditioned freezing.
source: Specifically, optogenetic stimulation of the aIC-amygdala pathway increased conditioned freezing, while optogenetic stimulation of the aIC-medial thalamus pathway decreased it.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the aIC-medial thalamus pathway decreased conditioned freezing.
source: Specifically, optogenetic stimulation of the aIC-amygdala pathway increased conditioned freezing, while optogenetic stimulation of the aIC-medial thalamus pathway decreased it.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pavlovian fear conditioning is believed to serve a crucial survival function in nature.
source: Pavlovian fear conditioning is believed to serve a crucial survival function in nature and is widely used as a preclinical model system to understand normal and abnormal fear behavior in humans (Kim and Jung, 2006; Maren and Fanselow, 1996; Armony et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pavlovian fear conditioning is widely used as a preclinical model system to understand normal and abnormal fear behavior in humans.
source: Pavlovian fear conditioning is believed to serve a crucial survival function in nature and is widely used as a preclinical model system to understand normal and abnormal fear behavior in humans (Kim and Jung, 2006; Maren and Fanselow, 1996; Armony et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Functional brain imaging studies consistently implicate the insular cortex (IC) in processing fear and anxiety in humans.
source: Functional brain imaging studies consistently implicate the insular cortex (IC) in processing fear and anxiety in humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to functional brain imaging studies.

claim: Healthy subjects show increased IC activity with fear conditioning.
source: Specifically, healthy subjects show increased IC activity with fear conditioning (Gottfried and Dolan, 2004; Klucken et al., 2009; Knight et al., 2009; Marschner et al., 2008; Morris and Dolan, 2004; Phelps et al., 2004), while patients with anxiety disorders exhibit even greater IC activity (Bruce et al., 2012; Yoon et al., 2017; Hoehn-Saric et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Patients with anxiety disorders exhibit even greater IC activity than healthy subjects.
source: Specifically, healthy subjects show increased IC activity with fear conditioning (Gottfried and Dolan, 2004; Klucken et al., 2009; Knight et al., 2009; Marschner et al., 2008; Morris and Dolan, 2004; Phelps et al., 2004), while patients with anxiety disorders exhibit even greater IC activity (Bruce et al., 2012; Yoon et al., 2017; Hoehn-Saric et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Re-exposure of rodents to a fear-conditioned context increases IC activity as measured by c-Fos or cytochrome oxidase staining.
source: For instance, re-exposure of rodents to a fear-conditioned context increases IC activity as measured by c-Fos or cytochrome oxidase staining (Beck and Fibiger, 1995; Bruchey and Gonzalez-Lima, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior animal studies.

claim: Microinjection of cobalt chloride, a non-selective synapse blocker, in the IC disrupts fear conditioning.
source: Additionally, microinjection of cobalt chloride, a non-selective synapse blocker, in the IC disrupts fear conditioning (Alves et al., 2013), and post-training electrolytic lesions of the IC attenuate the expression of conditioned fear (Brunzell and Kim, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Post-training electrolytic lesions of the IC attenuate the expression of conditioned fear.
source: Additionally, microinjection of cobalt chloride, a non-selective synapse blocker, in the IC disrupts fear conditioning (Alves et al., 2013), and post-training electrolytic lesions of the IC attenuate the expression of conditioned fear (Brunzell and Kim, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The IC is divided into the anterior IC (aIC) and posterior IC (pIC) by the middle cerebral artery.
source: Anatomically, the IC is divided into the anterior IC (aIC) and posterior IC (pIC) by the middle cerebral artery.
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The aIC and pIC are reciprocally connected.
source: Although they are reciprocally connected, the aIC and pIC have distinct connections with other brain regions (Gogolla, 2017; Shi and Cassell, 1998; Gehrlach et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The aIC and pIC have distinct connections with other brain regions.
source: Although they are reciprocally connected, the aIC and pIC have distinct connections with other brain regions (Gogolla, 2017; Shi and Cassell, 1998; Gehrlach et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The pIC receives inputs from the primary somatosensory thalamic nuclei.
source: Specifically, the pIC receives inputs from the primary somatosensory thalamic nuclei, while the aIC receives strong inputs from the prefrontal cortex and has reciprocal connections with higher order association thalamic nuclei, such as the mediodorsal thalamus.
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The aIC receives strong inputs from the prefrontal cortex.
source: Specifically, the pIC receives inputs from the primary somatosensory thalamic nuclei, while the aIC receives strong inputs from the prefrontal cortex and has reciprocal connections with higher order association thalamic nuclei, such as the mediodorsal thalamus.
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The aIC has reciprocal connections with higher order association thalamic nuclei, such as the mediodorsal thalamus.
source: Specifically, the pIC receives inputs from the primary somatosensory thalamic nuclei, while the aIC receives strong inputs from the prefrontal cortex and has reciprocal connections with higher order association thalamic nuclei, such as the mediodorsal thalamus.
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The aIC is ideally positioned to integrate high-level information to regulate behaviors.
source: Given its connections with cortical brain regions, the aIC is ideally positioned to integrate high-level information to regulate behaviors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the anatomical connectivity of the aIC.

claim: Both aIC and pIC have been implicated in fear conditioning.
source: Although both aIC and pIC have been implicated in fear conditioning (Alves et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2020; de Paiva et al., 2021; Casanova et al., 2016; Park et al., 2022), how the aIC connections to different brain regions modulate fear remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: 108 putative pyramidal neurons were analyzed from 11 mice.
source: Of the recorded neurons, we analyzed the activity of 108 putative pyramidal neurons (93% of total isolated neurons) from 11 mice, which were distinguished from putative interneurons (n=8 cells, 7% of total isolated neurons) based on the characteristics of their recorded action potentials (Figure 1D; see Methods for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data described in the manuscript.

claim: Putative pyramidal neurons comprised 93% of total isolated neurons.
source: Of the recorded neurons, we analyzed the activity of 108 putative pyramidal neurons (93% of total isolated neurons) from 11 mice, which were distinguished from putative interneurons (n=8 cells, 7% of total isolated neurons) based on the characteristics of their recorded action potentials (Figure 1D; see Methods for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data described in the manuscript.

claim: Putative interneurons comprised 7% of total isolated neurons.
source: Of the recorded neurons, we analyzed the activity of 108 putative pyramidal neurons (93% of total isolated neurons) from 11 mice, which were distinguished from putative interneurons (n=8 cells, 7% of total isolated neurons) based on the characteristics of their recorded action potentials (Figure 1D; see Methods for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data described in the manuscript.

claim: Auditory fear conditioned mice significantly increased their freezing behavior during the tone conditioned stimulus (CS) presentation.
source: As expected, the auditory fear conditioned mice significantly increased their freezing behavior during the tone conditioned stimulus (CS) presentation (Figure 1E, repeated-measures ANOVA, F(35,210) = 11.303, p<0.001), particularly during tone-on periods compared to tone-off periods (Figure 1F left, paired samples t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Control mice that did not undergo auditory fear conditioning showed virtually no freezing during the tone presentation.
source: In contrast, control mice that did not undergo auditory fear conditioning showed virtually no freezing during the tone presentation (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mean of all normalized pyramidal neuronal activities recorded in the aIC remained steady during the experiment in both groups.
source: The mean of all normalized (z-scored) pyramidal neuronal activities recorded in the aIC remained steady during the experiment in both groups (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The conditioned group showed no significant correlation between the normalized firing rate and freezing behavior.
source: The conditioned group showed no significant correlation between the normalized firing rate and freezing behavior, nor was there any difference in the mean firing rate between the tone-on and tone-off periods (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: There was no difference in the mean firing rate between the tone-on and tone-off periods in the conditioned group.
source: The conditioned group showed no significant correlation between the normalized firing rate and freezing behavior, nor was there any difference in the mean firing rate between the tone-on and tone-off periods (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The power of aIC local field potential in the <50 Hz frequency tended to be reduced in the conditioned group compared to the control during CS.
source: Similarly, the power of aIC local field potential in the <50 Hz frequency, which includes the theta frequency, tended to be reduced in the conditioned group compared to the control during CS (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by local field potential data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Theta frequency (6 Hz) was significantly reduced during, but not before, CS presentation in the conditioned group compared to the control.
source: Quantitative analysis revealed that theta frequency (6 Hz) was significantly reduced during, but not before, CS presentation in the conditioned group compared to the control (Figure 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by local field potential data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Among the neurons recorded from fear conditioned mice, 29.6% were responsive and 70.4% were non-responsive.
source: Among the neurons recorded from fear conditioned mice, 29.6% were responsive (n=32/108) and 70.4% were non-responsive (n=76/108; Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Among the responsive cells, there were proportionally more freezing-excite cells (65.6%) than freezing-inhibited cells (34.4%).
source: Among the responsive cells, there were proportionally more freezing-excite cells (n=21/32, 65.6%) than freezing-inhibited cells (n=11/32, 34.4%), but the trend was not statistically significant (binomial proportions test, p=0.11; Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The trend of more freezing-excited cells than freezing-inhibited cells was not statistically significant.
source: Among the responsive cells, there were proportionally more freezing-excite cells (n=21/32, 65.6%) than freezing-inhibited cells (n=11/32, 34.4%), but the trend was not statistically significant (binomial proportions test, p=0.11; Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Freezing-excited cells tended to be recorded in the middle and deep layers (L5 and 6).
source: The freezing-excited cells tended to be recorded in the middle and deep layers (L5 and 6; Figure 2C, red dots), while the freezing-inhibited cells tended to be recorded in the superficial and middle layers (L2/3, 4, and 5; Figure 2C, blue dots).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of recording locations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Freezing-inhibited cells tended to be recorded in the superficial and middle layers (L2/3, 4, and 5).
source: The freezing-excited cells tended to be recorded in the middle and deep layers (L5 and 6; Figure 2C, red dots), while the freezing-inhibited cells tended to be recorded in the superficial and middle layers (L2/3, 4, and 5; Figure 2C, blue dots).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of recording locations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Freezing-inhibited cells showed relatively higher tone-off firing rates, which decreased during tone presentation.
source: Freezing-inhibited cells showed relatively higher tone-off firing rates, which decreased during tone presentation (Figure 2D, conditioned upper).
evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Freezing-excited cells showed a lower tone-off firing rate that increased during tone presentation.
source: Freezing-excited cells, in contrast, showed a lower tone-off firing rate that increased during tone presentation (Figure 2D, conditioned lower).
evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Non-responsive cells showed an intermediate tone-off firing rate between those of the freezing-inhibited and freezing-excited cells and remained relatively constant throughout the recording.
source: The non-responsive cells, interestingly, showed an intermediate tone-off firing rate between those of the freezing-inhibited and freezing-excited cells and remained relatively constant throughout the recording (Figure 2D, conditioned middle).
evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The activities of the freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neurons were significantly correlated with freezing behavior in opposite directions.
source: Pearson's correlation coefficient between mean normalized firing rate and freezing of each neuronal response type revealed that the activities of the freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neurons were significantly correlated with freezing behavior in opposite directions (Figure 2F; freezing-excited cell r=0.81, p<0.05; freezing-inhibited cell r=–0.68, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: No correlation was found between non-responsive neurons and freezing behavior.
source: As expected, no correlation was found for the non-responsive neurons (r=0.13, p=0.44).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The tone-induced firing rate peaks of the freezing-inhibited and freezing-excited cells were significantly different.
source: The tone-induced firing rate peaks of the freezing-inhibited and freezing-excited cells were significantly different (Figure 2G, Mann-Whitney U Test, p<0.05); the freezing-inhibited cells peaked at 10.5 s, while the freezing-excited cells peaked at 17.6 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal analysis of neuronal recording data and statistical testing presented in the manuscript.

claim: The freezing-inhibited cells peaked at 10.5 s.
source: The tone-induced firing rate peaks of the freezing-inhibited and freezing-excited cells were significantly different (Figure 2G, Mann-Whitney U Test, p<0.05); the freezing-inhibited cells peaked at 10.5 s, while the freezing-excited cells peaked at 17.6 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal analysis of neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The freezing-excited cells peaked at 17.6 s.
source: The tone-induced firing rate peaks of the freezing-inhibited and freezing-excited cells were significantly different (Figure 2G, Mann-Whitney U Test, p<0.05); the freezing-inhibited cells peaked at 10.5 s, while the freezing-excited cells peaked at 17.6 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal analysis of neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: None of the recorded aIC neurons were tone-onset or tone-offset cells.
source: However, none of the recorded aIC neurons, neither the conditioned group's nor the control's, were tone-onset or tone-offset cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: None of the neuronal activity of control mice significantly correlated with the tone.
source: None of the neuronal activity of control mice (n=14 cells, 3 mice) significantly correlated with the tone (r=0.027, p=0.87), but a subset of aIC neurons in conditioned mice showed significant correlation with tone (freezing-excited cells, r=0.44, p<0.05, n=9; freezing-inhibited cells, r=−0.51, p<0.05, n=5).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A subset of aIC neurons in conditioned mice showed significant correlation with tone.
source: None of the neuronal activity of control mice (n=14 cells, 3 mice) significantly correlated with the tone (r=0.027, p=0.87), but a subset of aIC neurons in conditioned mice showed significant correlation with tone (freezing-excited cells, r=0.44, p<0.05, n=9; freezing-inhibited cells, r=−0.51, p<0.05, n=5).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: None of the recorded cells correlated with tone during fear extinction.
source: Interestingly, none of the recorded cells correlated with tone (Figure 2M).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of neuronal recording data during fear extinction presented in the manuscript.

claim: The freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited cells found in the aIC of fear-conditioned mice are highly correlated with freezing behavior, not tone.
source: Together, these results suggest that the freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited cells found in the aIC of fear-conditioned mice are highly correlated with freezing behavior, not tone.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation analyses comparing neuronal activity with freezing behavior and tone during fear expression and extinction.

claim: Neither activation of ChR2 nor NpHR3 triggered any aberrant behaviors in the open-field test.
source: Neither activation of ChR2 nor NpHR3 triggered any aberrant behaviors, and locomotion did not differ among groups (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the open-field test presented in the manuscript.

claim: Locomotion did not differ among groups in the open-field test with optogenetic stimulation.
source: Neither activation of ChR2 nor NpHR3 triggered any aberrant behaviors, and locomotion did not differ among groups (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the open-field test presented in the manuscript.

claim: ChR2 stimulation increased brain rhythms in the 20 Hz and 40 Hz range.
source: ChR2 stimulation increased brain rhythms in the 20 Hz and 40 Hz range (Figure 3D, spectrogram) because light stimulation was delivered at 20 Hz pulses.
evidence: This claim is supported by local field potential data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Continuous light for NpHR3 stimulation did not induce specific frequency modulation.
source: Continuous light was delivered for NpHR3 stimulation, so it did not induce specific frequency modulation (Figure 3E, spectrogram).
evidence: This claim is supported by local field potential data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Optostimulation of the aIC neurons did not induce aberrant seizure-like synchronized activities.
source: Simultaneous local field potential (LFP) and single unit analysis before, during, and after optical stimulations confirmed that optostimulation of the aIC neurons did not induce aberrant seizure-like synchronized activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by simultaneous LFP and single unit recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: During a 30 s tone +optostimulation, there was no difference in freezing behavior among groups.
source: During a 30 s tone +optostimulation, there was no difference in freezing behavior among groups (Figure 3G; Kruskal-Wallis, H(2) = 2.489, p=0.288).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: During the tone-off sessions, freezing behavior among groups differed significantly.
source: However, during the tone-off sessions, freezing behavior among groups differed significantly (Figure 3G; Kruskal-Wallis, H(2) = 22.937, p=0.000; post hoc Mann-Whitney, ChR2 vs. control p=0.000; NpHR vs. control p=0.019).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Conditioned freezing responses of the ChR2 group were sustained even after tone +optostimulation ended, and tended to accumulate with repeated stimulations, particularly during the tone-off sessions.
source: Conditioned freezing responses of the ChR2 group were sustained even after tone +optostimulation ended, and tended to accumulate with repeated stimulations, particularly during the tone-off sessions.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the NpHR3 group, freezing immediately decreased after tone +optostimulation ended.
source: In the NpHR3 group, freezing immediately decreased after tone +optostimulation ended (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition of aIC pyramidal neurons (NpHR3) reduced the freezing level between the first and the last tone +optostimulation.
source: When comparing the freezing behavior of each group during their first and last tone +optostimulation trials, inhibition of aIC pyramidal neurons (NpHR3) reduced the freezing level between the first and the last tone +optostimulation (Figure 3H, left; Wilcoxon signed test, p=0.063).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: During the tone-off period, the ChR2 group significantly increased freezing after the last stimulation compared to the first.
source: During the tone-off period, the ChR2 group significantly increased freezing after the last stimulation compared to the first (Figure 3H, right; Wilcoxon signed test, **p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Group differences in fear expression were absent in the experiment carried out without optostimulation.
source: These group differences in fear expression were absent in the experiment carried out without optostimulation (ANOVA group effect: F(2,30) = 1.076, p=0.354; Figure 3I and J), confirming that group differences in fear expression were induced by the activation or inhibition of pyramidal neurons in the aIC.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Group differences in fear expression were induced by the activation or inhibition of pyramidal neurons in the aIC.
source: These group differences in fear expression were absent in the experiment carried out without optostimulation (ANOVA group effect: F(2,30) = 1.076, p=0.354; Figure 3I and J), confirming that group differences in fear expression were induced by the activation or inhibition of pyramidal neurons in the aIC.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of behavioral results with and without optostimulation.

claim: None of the neurons in the aIC expressed both green and red fluorophores.
source: Surprisingly, none of the neurons in the aIC expressed both green and red fluorophores, suggesting that non-overlapping populations of aIC neurons project to the medial dorsal thalamus and the amygdala (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The aIC neurons projecting to the medial dorsal thalamus appeared mainly in the deep layers (approximately layer 6).
source: The neurons projecting to the medial dorsal thalamus and the amygdala were also located in different layers within the aIC; the aIC neurons projecting to the medial dorsal thalamus appeared mainly in the deep layers (approximately layer 6), while the aIC neurons projecting to the amygdala appeared in a relatively more superficial layer (approximately layer 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of retrograde tracing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The aIC neurons projecting to the amygdala appeared in a relatively more superficial layer (approximately layer 5).
source: The neurons projecting to the medial dorsal thalamus and the amygdala were also located in different layers within the aIC; the aIC neurons projecting to the medial dorsal thalamus appeared mainly in the deep layers (approximately layer 6), while the aIC neurons projecting to the amygdala appeared in a relatively more superficial layer (approximately layer 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of retrograde tracing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The number of aIC neurons projecting to the medial dorsal thalamus was greater than those projecting to the amygdala.
source: The number of aIC neurons projecting to the medial dorsal thalamus was greater than those projecting to the amygdala even though they were populated in a more restricted area (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of retrograde tracing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The aIC→medial thalamus neurons could be freezing-excited cells.
source: Collectively, data suggest that the aIC→medial thalamus neurons could be freezing-excited cells, while the aIC→amygdala neurons may be freezing-inhibited cells.
evidence: This claim is speculated based on the comparison of recording locations and tracing results.

claim: The aIC→amygdala neurons may be freezing-inhibited cells.
source: Collectively, data suggest that the aIC→medial thalamus neurons could be freezing-excited cells, while the aIC→amygdala neurons may be freezing-inhibited cells.
evidence: This claim is speculated based on the comparison of recording locations and tracing results.

claim: The aIC projection to the thalamus terminated mainly in the MD and CM regions.
source: As shown in the sample expression patterns, the aIC projection to the thalamus terminated mainly in the MD and CM regions (Figure 5B), while the aIC projection to the amygdala terminated mainly in the BLA and CeA (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of viral expression patterns presented in the manuscript.

claim: The aIC projection to the amygdala terminated mainly in the BLA and CeA.
source: As shown in the sample expression patterns, the aIC projection to the thalamus terminated mainly in the MD and CM regions (Figure 5B), while the aIC projection to the amygdala terminated mainly in the BLA and CeA (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of viral expression patterns presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activating the aIC→medial thalamus projection significantly reduced freezing compared to the control.
source: While activating the aIC→medial thalamus projection significantly reduced freezing compared to the control (Figure 5C, blue line; repeated measures ANOVA, F(1, 17)=10.666, *** p<0.001), activating the aIC→amygdala projection significantly enhanced freezing compared to the control (Figure 5G, red line; repeated measures ANOVA, F(1, 12)=23.663, *** p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic manipulation data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activating the aIC→amygdala projection significantly enhanced freezing compared to the control.
source: While activating the aIC→medial thalamus projection significantly reduced freezing compared to the control (Figure 5C, blue line; repeated measures ANOVA, F(1, 17)=10.666, *** p<0.001), activating the aIC→amygdala projection significantly enhanced freezing compared to the control (Figure 5G, red line; repeated measures ANOVA, F(1, 12)=23.663, *** p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic manipulation data and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: When opto-stimulation was turned off, and only the conditioned tone was delivered (retrieval test), there were no differences in the freezing level between groups.
source: Also, when opto-stimulation was turned off, and only the conditioned tone was delivered (retrieval test), there were no differences in the freezing level between groups (Figure 5C and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the retrieval test presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of neither the aIC→medial thalamus nor the aIC→amygdala projection produced any lasting behavioral effects between light stimulations.
source: In addition, we compared freezing levels of tone +optostim and tone-off periods to assess whether activation of these pathways produces a lasting effect on behavior. Unlike the phenomenon observed in aIC activation with ChR2 (Figure 3F), activation of neither the aIC→medial thalamus nor the aIC→amygdala projection produced any lasting behavioral effects between light stimulations (Figure 5D and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data comparing tone+optostim and tone-off periods presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the pIC, a significantly larger population of excitatory neurons was reported compared to inhibitory neurons.
source: In the pIC, a significantly larger population of excitatory neurons was reported compared to inhibitory neurons (Casanova et al., 2018), but in the aIC, we found approximately equal number of freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: In the aIC, approximately equal number of freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neurons were found.
source: In the pIC, a significantly larger population of excitatory neurons was reported compared to inhibitory neurons (Casanova et al., 2018), but in the aIC, we found approximately equal number of freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: An E/I imbalance has been linked to various disorders, such as epilepsy, schizophrenia, and autism spectrum disorder.
source: An E/I imbalance has been linked to various disorders, such as epilepsy, schizophrenia, and autism spectrum disorder (Yizhar et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Group activity of neurons in the pIC exhibited fear state dependent activity changes—decreased activity with high fear behavior and increased activity with lower fear behavior.
source: Group activity of neurons in the pIC measured with fiberphotometry, interestingly, exhibited fear state dependent activity changes—decreased activity with high fear behavior and increased activity with lower fear behavior (Klein et al., 2021)—suggesting that group activity of the pIC may be involved in maintaining appropriate level of fear behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Group activity of the pIC may be involved in maintaining appropriate level of fear behavior.
source: Group activity of neurons in the pIC measured with fiberphotometry, interestingly, exhibited fear state dependent activity changes—decreased activity with high fear behavior and increased activity with lower fear behavior (Klein et al., 2021)—suggesting that group activity of the pIC may be involved in maintaining appropriate level of fear behavior.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of fear state dependent activity changes in the pIC.

claim: The aIC maintains E/I balance at the cellular activity level when processing fear, possibly by activating different circuits.
source: This study has not investigated whether the aIC also show fear state dependent changes in group neuronal activities; however, approximately equal number of neurons were freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neuron found in our study suggests that the aIC maintains E/I balance at the cellular activity level when processing fear, possibly by activating different circuits.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the finding of approximately equal numbers of freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neurons.

claim: Temporal differences in the arrival of excitatory and inhibitory inputs can create a time window for local signals to be transmitted while maintaining the global E/I balance.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that temporal differences in the arrival of excitatory and inhibitory inputs can create a time window for local signals to be transmitted while maintaining the global E/I balance (Vogels and Abbott, 2009; Bhatia et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The observed differences in the temporal activity of the freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited aIC cells may provide a window for orchestrating signal gating and processing.
source: We hypothesize that the observed differences in the temporal activity of the freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited aIC cells may provide such a window for orchestrating signal gating and processing.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the observed temporal differences in neuronal activity.

claim: The aIC may play a critical role in regulating the balance between excitation and inhibition during fear conditioning.
source: This suggests that the aIC may play a critical role in regulating the balance between excitation and inhibition during fear conditioning.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the findings about temporal differences in neuronal activity and E/I balance.

claim: Group activity of aIC neurons, but not that of the pIC, increased when mice explored anxiogenic space.
source: Another distinction between the aIC and pIC may be related with anxiety, as a recent study showed that group activity of aIC neurons, but not that of the pIC, increased when mice explored anxiogenic space (open arms in an elevated plus maze, center of an open field box) (Nicolas et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: The aIC is involved in stress-induced anxiety and neuronal activity correlated with stress-induced defensive behavior (burying).
source: Our previous study also showed that the aIC is involved in stress-induced anxiety and that neuronal activity correlated with stress-induced defensive behavior (burying) (Park et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous study.

claim: Human studies implicated the activity of the aIC to be more correlated with subjective fear experience.
source: Since human studies implicated the activity of the aIC to be more correlated with subjective fear experience (Gogolla, 2017; Uddin et al., 2017; Terasawa et al., 2013; Torrence et al., 2019), the aIC may be more specialized in regulating subjective fear and collectively integrating both anxiety and fear information.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior human studies.

claim: The aIC may be more specialized in regulating subjective fear and collectively integrating both anxiety and fear information.
source: Since human studies implicated the activity of the aIC to be more correlated with subjective fear experience (Gogolla, 2017; Uddin et al., 2017; Terasawa et al., 2013; Torrence et al., 2019), the aIC may be more specialized in regulating subjective fear and collectively integrating both anxiety and fear information.
evidence: This claim is inferred from human studies and the authors' findings about aIC involvement in anxiety and fear.

claim: Freezing-inhibited cells may receive input from the prefrontal cortex.
source: For instance, freezing-inhibited cells may receive input from the prefrontal cortex since whole-brain connectivity analysis of the IC indicated that the prefrontal cortex provides more inputs to inhibitory neurons in the aIC than to excitatory neurons (Gehrlach et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is speculated based on whole-brain connectivity analysis cited from prior literature.

claim: Freezing-excited cells may receive input from the amygdala.
source: Conversely, freezing-excited cells may receive input from the amygdala, as the amygdala provides more input to excitatory neurons in the aIC than inhibitory neurons (Gehrlach et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is speculated based on whole-brain connectivity analysis cited from prior literature.

claim: Specifically targeting freezing-inhibited or freezing-excited cells for neuromodulation may not be necessary to have a therapeutic effect.
source: These findings have significant clinical implications since they suggest that specifically targeting freezing-inhibited or freezing-excited cells for neuromodulation may not be necessary to have a therapeutic effect.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the finding that controlling total aIC output can bidirectionally modulate fear behavior.

claim: Merely controlling the total output of the aIC may be enough to regulate fear and anxiety disorders.
source: Even though the aIC has fine microcircuitry and intricate connections with many brain regions, merely controlling the total output of the aIC may be enough to regulate fear and anxiety disorders.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the optogenetic manipulation results showing bidirectional modulation of fear behavior.

claim: Brief excitation or inhibition of aIC pyramidal neurons had a residual effect on behavior during the inter-trial period when optic stimulation was off.
source: During the aIC optogenetic stimulation, we observed a phenomenon where brief excitation or inhibition of aIC pyramidal neurons had a residual effect on behavior during the inter-trial period when optic stimulation was off.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from optogenetic experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Another study reports the cumulative effects of optical activation of ChR2-expressing neurons on freezing behavior even after optic stimulation ended.
source: Another study also reports the cumulative effects of optical activation of ChR2-expressing neurons on freezing behavior even after optic stimulation ended (Han et al., 2015), supporting that it can happen.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The residual effect is not due to seizure produced by optostimulations.
source: Although further studies will be necessary to verify what causes this phenomenon, our single unit recording and local field potential analysis during optostimulation support that it is not due to seizure produced by optostimulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by single unit and LFP analysis during optostimulation presented in the manuscript.

claim: The residual effect may occur due to the recruitment of several brain areas modulated by the aIC neurons.
source: It may occur due to the recruitment of several brain areas modulated by the aIC neurons since activating a more specific circuit, the aIC→medial thalamus or the aIC→amygdala projection, did not produce any lasting effects between light stimulations.
evidence: This claim is speculated based on the comparison of effects from general aIC activation versus specific pathway activation.

claim: Activation or inhibition of the aIC may promote or reduce activation of a recurrent circuit that controls behavior.
source: Activation or inhibition of the aIC may promote or reduce activation of a recurrent circuit that controls behavior, especially since the aIC has connections with motor-related brain regions (Gehrlach et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is speculated based on the aIC's connections with motor-related brain regions.

claim: Amygdala activation promotes fear responses.
source: Our results are consistent with previous studies reporting that amygdala activation promotes fear responses (Johansen et al., 2010), while thalamus activation, especially in the burst firing mode of the MD, reduces fear responses (Lee et al., 2011; Baek et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Thalamus activation, especially in the burst firing mode of the MD, reduces fear responses.
source: Our results are consistent with previous studies reporting that amygdala activation promotes fear responses (Johansen et al., 2010), while thalamus activation, especially in the burst firing mode of the MD, reduces fear responses (Lee et al., 2011; Baek et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Terminal optogenetic stimulation could produce antidromic activation.
source: Although terminal optogenetic stimulation could produce antidromic activation (Li et al., 2018), it only activates a subset of aIC neurons projecting to the areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Terminal optogenetic stimulation only activates a subset of aIC neurons projecting to the target areas.
source: Although terminal optogenetic stimulation could produce antidromic activation (Li et al., 2018), it only activates a subset of aIC neurons projecting to the areas.
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of terminal optogenetic stimulation.

claim: This study demonstrates for the first time that controlling distinct aIC outputs bidirectionally regulate fear behaviors.
source: Our study, therefore, demonstrates for the first time that controlling distinct aIC outputs bidirectionally regulate fear behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by the optogenetic manipulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: If medial thalamus projecting neurons are freezing-excited cells and amygdala projecting neurons are freezing-inhibited cells, then the activity of the aIC neurons would work as a mechanism to reduce overexpression of fear.
source: Although we do not have a direct link between single-unit recording and aIC projections, the recording locations of the freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited cells suggest that medial thalamus projecting neurons could be freezing-excited cells while the amygdala projecting neurons may be freezing-inhibited cells. If so, then the activity of the aIC neurons would work as a mechanism to reduce overexpression of fear.
evidence: This claim is speculated based on the comparison of recording locations and projection patterns.

claim: The insular→central amygdala and the insula→nucleus accumbens differentially regulated fear.
source: Similar to our findings, the insular→central amygdala and the insula→nucleus accumbens differentially regulated fear (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The insular cortex is extensively connected with various brain regions.
source: Since the insular cortex is extensively connected with various brain regions (Gehrlach et al., 2020), several redundant circuits may be present in the aIC to fine-tune fear behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Several redundant circuits may be present in the aIC to fine-tune fear behavior.
source: Since the insular cortex is extensively connected with various brain regions (Gehrlach et al., 2020), several redundant circuits may be present in the aIC to fine-tune fear behavior.
evidence: This claim is speculated based on the extensive connectivity of the insular cortex.

claim: Many studies report that there is no biological sex difference in cued fear conditioning.
source: Although many studies report that there is no biological sex difference in cued fear conditioning (Day and Stevenson, 2020), the main experimental paradigm used in this study, it does not mean that the underlying brain circuit mechanism would also be similar.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The underlying brain circuit mechanism for cued fear conditioning may not be similar between sexes.
source: Although many studies report that there is no biological sex difference in cued fear conditioning (Day and Stevenson, 2020), the main experimental paradigm used in this study, it does not mean that the underlying brain circuit mechanism would also be similar.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that behavioral similarity does not necessarily imply circuit similarity.

claim: The bidirectional fear modulation by aIC→medial thalamus or the aIC→amygdala projections may be different in female mice.
source: The bidirectional fear modulation by aIC→medial thalamus or the aIC→amygdala projections may be different in female mice, as some studies report reduced cued fear extinction in females (Day and Stevenson, 2020).
evidence: This claim is speculated based on reported sex differences in fear extinction.

claim: Some studies report reduced cued fear extinction in females.
source: The bidirectional fear modulation by aIC→medial thalamus or the aIC→amygdala projections may be different in female mice, as some studies report reduced cued fear extinction in females (Day and Stevenson, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The aIC regulates conditioned fear behaviors through bidirectional control on multiple levels.
source: In conclusion, our study provides evidence that the aIC regulates conditioned fear behaviors through bidirectional control on multiple levels, with the balance of freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neuronal activity operating at the local circuit level and different populations of neurons projecting to different brain regions exerting additional control.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined findings from single-unit recordings, optogenetic manipulations, and neural tracing presented in the manuscript.

claim: The balance of freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neuronal activity operates at the local circuit level.
source: In conclusion, our study provides evidence that the aIC regulates conditioned fear behaviors through bidirectional control on multiple levels, with the balance of freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neuronal activity operating at the local circuit level and different populations of neurons projecting to different brain regions exerting additional control.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-unit recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Different populations of neurons projecting to different brain regions exert additional control over fear behavior.
source: In conclusion, our study provides evidence that the aIC regulates conditioned fear behaviors through bidirectional control on multiple levels, with the balance of freezing-excited and freezing-inhibited neuronal activity operating at the local circuit level and different populations of neurons projecting to different brain regions exerting additional control.
evidence: This claim is supported by neural tracing and optogenetic manipulation data presented in the manuscript.
